lines.cap: Right now, inside trillions of your cells, something is quietly burning your breakfast.
No flames, no smoke, and nothing hot enough to cook you.
It's called **respiration**: the chemical reaction that releases the energy stored in food, so every cell can stay alive.
Let's follow a sugar called **glucose** into a cell, find out where its energy goes, and see what happens when oxygen runs out.
First, one thing to get straight: respiration is **not** the same as breathing.
**Breathing**, which scientists call **ventilation**, moves air in and out of your lungs. It's a physical process, done by muscles, your ribs and your diaphragm.
**Respiration** is a **chemical reaction** inside cells. It releases energy from glucose.
It happens in **every** living cell, all the time: in your skin, your brain and your muscles, and in plants and bacteria too.
So it doesn't need lungs. A goldfish has gills, and a tree has no lungs at all, yet every one of their cells is respiring right now.
Use the right word: respiration **releases** energy. It never makes or creates energy, because energy can't be created.
The chemical energy stored in glucose is simply **transferred** into forms the cell can use.
And the glucose? Animals get it by **digesting food**. Plants make their own by **photosynthesis**.
The main type of respiration uses oxygen. It's called **aerobic** respiration: aerobic means 'with air', or with oxygen.
Here's the word equation: **glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water**, and energy is released.
To remember the order, think: **G**lad **O**wls **C**arry **W**et **E**ggs. Glucose, oxygen, carbon dioxide, water, energy.
Glucose and oxygen are the **reactants**: what goes in. Carbon dioxide and water are the **products**: what comes out.
Energy goes in brackets, because it's released. It isn't a chemical substance.
Now the symbol equation: **C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O**
Let's check it's balanced. On the left: **6** carbon atoms, **12** hydrogen atoms and **18** oxygen atoms: 6 from glucose and 12 from the oxygen.
Now watch the atoms rearrange.
On the right: still **6** carbons, **12** hydrogens and **18** oxygens, now shared between carbon dioxide and water. No atoms are lost or made, so **mass is conserved**.
Aerobic respiration releases **a large amount of energy** from each glucose. That's why it's the main type in humans, animals and plants.
Your **blood** brings oxygen to your cells, and carries the waste carbon dioxide back to your lungs, so you can breathe it out.
So where does aerobic respiration happen? Inside tiny structures called **mitochondria**. Just one is called a **mitochondrion**.
They're often called the **powerhouses** of the cell, because this is where most of the energy is released.
Look inside one. The inner membrane is folded, again and again.
Unfold it, and it's far longer. The folds give a **large surface area** for the reactions of respiration.
The more active a cell is, the **more mitochondria** it has.
**Muscle cells** are packed with them, because contracting muscles need lots of energy.
**Sperm cells** have many in their middle section, to power the tail for swimming.
**Liver cells** are full of them, because the liver carries out lots of energy-hungry reactions.
But a **fat-storage cell** needs little energy, so it has only a few.
So if you see lots of mitochondria, you can predict a **high energy demand**.
Don't mix them up with chloroplasts. **Photosynthesis** happens in **chloroplasts**; **respiration** happens in **mitochondria**.
A bonus fact: scientists think mitochondria were once free-living **bacteria** that moved into bigger cells long ago. They even have their own **DNA**.

chapters.title: What the energy is used for

lines.cap: What's all that energy for? It powers the **life processes** that keep an organism alive.
**Movement**: muscles contracting. That's why exercising muscles respire faster.
**Growth**: building new cells and tissues, to get bigger or to repair damage.
**Making big molecules**: joining small molecules into large ones, like building proteins from amino acids.
**Active transport**: moving substances across cell membranes **against a concentration gradient**, like a root taking in minerals from the soil.
**Keeping warm**: mammals and birds use some of the energy as heat, to keep a steady body temperature.
And **nerve impulses**, plus lots of other jobs inside cells.
Not all of the energy is useful. Some is always **transferred to the surroundings as heat**. For mammals and birds, though, that heat keeps them warm.
That's why a small bird must eat almost all day in cold weather, while a lizard the same size can go much longer without food.
And your brain is only about **2%** of your body mass, yet it uses around **a fifth** of your energy, even while you sleep.
Sometimes your muscles need energy faster than your blood can deliver oxygen. Think of a flat-out sprint.
When there isn't enough oxygen, muscle cells switch to **anaerobic** respiration. The prefix **an-** means **absent**: no oxygen.
The word equation is: **glucose → lactic acid**, and a little energy is released.
It releases **much less energy** than aerobic respiration, because the glucose is only **partly** broken down.
And it makes **no carbon dioxide** and no water. Just lactic acid.
Lactic acid builds up in the muscles. It's linked to the burning feeling, and to **muscle fatigue**, when muscles get tired and ache.
Afterwards, your body needs extra oxygen to break the lactic acid down. This is called the **oxygen debt**.
That's why you keep panting, and your heart keeps pounding, for a while after you stop.
So a sprinter relies far more on anaerobic respiration than a marathon runner, and that's why no one can sprint flat out for very long.
Scientists now know the burn is a bit more complicated, and next-day soreness is mostly tiny muscle damage. But for your exam: **lactic acid**, **fatigue** and **oxygen debt**.
**Yeast** is a single-celled fungus. When yeast respires without oxygen, it's called **fermentation**.
Its products are different from ours: **glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide**, and a little energy is released.
**Ethanol** is the alcohol in alcoholic drinks.
To remember who makes what: **L**azy **A**thletes, **E**nergetic **Y**east. **L**actic acid for athletes, **e**thanol for yeast.
People have used fermentation for thousands of years.
In **bread-making**, yeast in the dough makes **carbon dioxide** gas, and the bubbles make the dough **rise**.
In the oven, the ethanol evaporates, but the holes stay behind, so the bread is light and airy.
In **brewing** and wine-making, the **ethanol** makes the alcoholic drink, and the carbon dioxide can make it fizzy.
Fermentation releases only a little energy, but for bakers and brewers it's the **products** that matter.
Try it at home: warm water, sugar and yeast in a bottle, with a balloon stretched over the top. In half an hour or so, the balloon starts to fill with **carbon dioxide**.
Let's put them side by side. Both start with **glucose**, and both release energy. They differ in three ways: **oxygen**, **energy** and **products**.
**Aerobic**: uses oxygen, releases **a lot** of energy, and makes **carbon dioxide and water**.
**Anaerobic, in humans**: no oxygen, releases **a little** energy, and makes **lactic acid**.
**Anaerobic, in yeast**: no oxygen, releases **a little** energy, and makes **ethanol and carbon dioxide**.
Why so much more energy from aerobic? Because the glucose is **completely** broken down.
In anaerobic respiration it's only **partly** broken down, so most of its energy stays **locked inside** the lactic acid or the ethanol.
So anaerobic respiration isn't better just because it works without oxygen. It's a **short-term backup**.
Three processes often get muddled up: **respiration**, **photosynthesis** and **breathing**.
Respiration and photosynthesis are roughly **opposites**.
Respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, **releasing** energy. It happens in **all** living cells, **all the time**.
Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, **storing** energy from light. It happens only in **green plant cells** with chlorophyll, and only **in the light**.
A green plant does both. And here's the big one: plants **respire all the time**, day and night, in every living cell: roots, stems, flowers and leaves.
In bright light, photosynthesis runs faster than respiration, so overall the plant takes in **carbon dioxide** and gives out **oxygen**.
At night there's no photosynthesis, so only respiration shows: the plant takes in **oxygen** and gives out **carbon dioxide**.
And breathing? **Breathing**, or **ventilation**, is the muscular movement of air in and out of the lungs. It isn't a chemical reaction.
Breathing **supplies** the oxygen for aerobic respiration, and **removes** the carbon dioxide it makes. Linked, but not the same.
Remember: **C**ells **R**espire, **L**ungs **V**entilate.
We can't see respiration directly, so experiments detect its **products** and effects.
Test one: carbon dioxide. **Limewater** turns from clear to **milky**, or cloudy, when carbon dioxide bubbles through it.
Bubble air you breathe **in** through one tube, and air you breathe **out** through another. The breathed-out air turns the limewater milky much faster, because respiration has added carbon dioxide.
Test two: heat. Put living, **germinating peas** in one vacuum flask, and **boiled**, dead peas in another, each with a thermometer.
Over a few days, the flask of living seeds gets **warmer**, because respiration releases heat. Dead seeds can't respire, so their temperature doesn't rise.
The boiled seeds are the **control**. And washing the seeds in **disinfectant** first stops microbes from making heat instead.

Test three: oxygen. Living things in a sealed tube use up oxygen. In a **respirometer**, a chemical soaks up the carbon dioxide, so a drop of coloured liquid creeps along the tube as the oxygen is used.
Whatever you test, make it a **fair test**: change just one variable, keep everything else the same, and include a **control** to compare with.

chapters.title: Recap: memory hooks and exam traps

lines.cap: Let's lock it all in.
**Glad Owls Carry Wet Eggs**: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy).
**Aerobic** means with oxygen, while **an**aerobic means without it.
**Lazy Athletes, Energetic Yeast**: lactic acid in humans; ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast.
**Cells Respire, Lungs Ventilate.**
Now, five exam traps to avoid.
One: respiration **releases** energy. It doesn't make it.
Two: write **(+ energy)** in your equations, and check the **sixes** in the symbol equation.
Three: anaerobic respiration in humans makes **lactic acid only**. No carbon dioxide.
Four: plants respire **all the time**, not just at night.
Five: anaerobic respiration releases **less** energy than aerobic, not more.
Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
Where in the cell does aerobic respiration happen?
In the **mitochondria**.
What does yeast make when it respires without oxygen?
**Ethanol and carbon dioxide.**
What happens to limewater when carbon dioxide bubbles through it?
It turns from clear to **milky**.
Why do you keep panting after a sprint?
To take in extra oxygen and repay the **oxygen debt**, breaking down the lactic acid.
True or false: plants only respire at night.
**False.** Plants respire all the time, day and night.
Brilliant work. Now try the Respiration quiz in your Science Lab, to lock it in.
